extracted.intended_audience: school librarians and classroom teachers (elementary and secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: A classroom lesson idea that uses single-panel (gag) cartoons to teach scriptwriting by having students combine formal-sounding captions with absurd visuals; intended for elementary and secondary students. The activity scaffolds components of comics scripts (art description + caption) and includes brainstorming, scripting, production, and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a simple, producible medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a simple, intuitive medium that's easy to script and then produce the results of that script: comics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes using comics to make scriptwriting accessible rather than technical; comics let students both write and quickly realize their scripts, lowering barriers to entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match format to student age/level
rubrics_metrics.description: With very young students teach 'beginning-middle-end' with three-panel newspaper-style comic strips; for slightly older elementary and secondary students introduce the pared-down single-panel (gag) cartoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt the complexity of the comics format to student developmental level: 3-panel strips for 1st graders, single-panel gag cartoons for older students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activate prior knowledge and model the form
rubrics_metrics.description: Have students share what they know about the form, perhaps reviewing what they may have learned about political cartoons in social studies or history classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible provide an example or two; some students may be able to quickly sketch a cartoon from memory on the board. Use discussion and modeling to orient students to conventions of gag cartoons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach comics as the combination of text plus art
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out that gag cartoons almost always contain a caption, called the gag line, and can also feature text in the art itself (labels, signs) and sometimes word balloons. The key idea is that it’s the combination of text plus art that constitutes the comics medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the lesson on the two different textual modes involved in comics and how a script brings them together to create meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrasting formal captions and absurd visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: One group should brainstorm sentence-starters in the imperative mood that sound formal and 'official' (such as 'Please utilize all due caution . . .', 'Refrain from unruly behavior while . . .'). The second group should brainstorm humorous anthropomorphic images and characters (a talking banana or pickle, or a 'funny animal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The humor of the gag arises from the contrast between the serious/formal caption language and the absurd or anthropomorphic visual; deliberately pair the two to generate gags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption style: imperative, formal 'gag line'
rubrics_metrics.description: For the caption, students need only complete the sentence-starters; captions are typically the gag line and can be written in the imperative mood with a formal tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sentence-starters that sound 'official' to scaffold students' creation of humorous completions; keep caption-writing concise so it functions as the punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art portion: describe visuals that set up the gag
rubrics_metrics.description: For the art portion of the script, students should describe an image based on the funny visuals already provided—one that sets up the caption’s gag line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students sketch or describe anthropomorphic characters or absurd scenes on the board or easel; the art description should clearly set up the caption/punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a simple two-part script format (Description of Art / Caption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Script using the simple format: Description of Art: [describe image] Caption: [complete sentence-starter].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-part format reduces comics scripting to its simplest elements and mirrors professional comics scripting by separating text and visual instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share, produce, and reflect
rubrics_metrics.description: Have groups share these mini-scripts by reading them aloud, choose one or more to 'produce' by drawing the art and lettering the caption beneath it, then have students reflect on how the process and results might be different if they were free to make up both the visuals and the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral sharing surfaces what works; producing selected scripts as drawings shows the realization of a script; guided reflection connects the classroom activity to real-world scriptwriting choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect the exercise to broader scriptwriting practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain that this activity reflects the creative process used in any type of comics boiled down to its simplest elements and that scriptwriting combines creative-writing and practical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the completed activity as a bridge: once students grasp combining text and art, they are ready to try their hand at a range of scripts (comics, graphic novels, other script forms).
